parole.significato: diamonds (one of the four suits of playing cards, marked with the symbol ♦)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Czech bubny m pl (“bells in German playing cards”), plural of buben m (“drum”) cognate to the Russian бу́бен (búben, “tambourine”) calquing German Schellen, better known as kule f pl (literally “bullets”) in Czech.

parole.significato: dwarf (various senses), midget, gnome, pygmy, manikin, elf
parole.testo: Borrowed from Czech karel, karlík or Polish karlę, karzeł, karlik, all from Old High German karal, whence Middle High German karl (“little boy”) and German Kerl (“young man”). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *karilaz.
Borrowed from Czech kalhotky, ultimately from Latin caliga.
Borrowed from Czech král. Doublet of король (korolʹ).
Borrowed from Czech polka (“half-step dance”), variant of půlka (“a half”), diminutive of půl (“a half”) (Russian пол- (pol-)), from Proto-Slavic *polъ, further origin uncertain.

parole.significato: contemporary, age-mate (one who is the same age as another)

Originally from Saint Petersburg criminal argot. According to Vasmer, perhaps related to Italian schietto (“clear, frank”). According to Trubachyov, borrowed from Czech škеtа (“fool”).
